en: The Commentary on the *Mahāyāna Śālistamba Sūtra* Compiled by the Śramaṇa Facheng.
In preparing to explain this sūtra, it is analyzed in general through five sections: first, establishing the tenet; second, clarifying the refuge...
The Three Illuminations return to their divisions;
the Fourfold Eloquence returns to the Repository.
Fifth, the explanation:
these five meanings are based upon the sūtras and treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Now, this shall be briefly explained.
First, regarding the statement "establishing the tenet":
it refers to the views and tenets of the world.
Although they are immeasurable,
to state the essentials,
they do not exceed two kinds.
First, the external;
second, the internal.
Regarding those external schools, there are ninety-six views.
To summarize, there are sixteen treatises.
Therefore, within the "Three Bases with Vitarka and Vicāra" and so forth in the *Maulī Bhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it says: "The uddāna states:"
They cling to the view that the effect exists within the cause;
they manifest [the belief in] the existence of past and future;
and they hold that the self is eternal and that past actions are the cause.
The dharmas of harming such as [the view of] mastery are boundless delusions of pride;
they involve reckoning [things] as causeless, nihilistic, and empty.
Regarding the "Sixteen Heterodox Doctrines" [known as] "Supreme Pure Auspiciousness," the prose commentary explains as follows:
One should understand that improper mental attention is revealed through sixteen types of divergent views.
What are these sixteen?
1. The theory that the effect exists within the cause;
2. The theory that [the effect] is manifested from conditions;
3. The theory that the past and future are substantially real.
Fourth, the doctrine of the self;
fifth, the doctrine of eternalism;
sixth, the doctrine of past actions as the cause.
Seventh, the theory that Īśvara and others are the creator;
eighth, the theory that violence constitutes the true dharma;
ninth, the theory of finitude and infinitude.
10. The doctrine of immortality and arrogance;
11. The doctrine of the view of no cause;
12. The doctrine of the view of annihilation.
13. The doctrine of the view of emptiness;
14. The doctrine of false imputation of supremacy;
15. The doctrine of false imputation of purity.
Sixteenth, the treatises on the false imputation of auspiciousness.
All such treatises ultimately converge upon two types of views: first, nihilism;
[second, eternalism].
The two [types of] permanence.
The textual elaborations for establishing and refuting these sixteen arguments are not recounted here due to their prolixity;
they are explained extensively in the second [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding what is called the "internal schools," generally speaking, there are two types:
first, the Hīnayāna school.
Second is the Mahāyāna school.
Regarding what is called the Hīnayāna school, there was no difference among the masters while they were studying under the same teacher;
however, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, because the personal views of various masters differed, it subsequently split into many schools.
There are some treatises that explain both the root and the branches together as twenty-two;
others explain them such that the root and branches consist of twenty sections,
as described in detail in the two versions of the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*.
Although there are many such sectarian tenets within the Hīnayāna,
they ultimately all converge upon a single view.
What is this one [view]?
This refers to the adherence to the view that all phenomena possess an intrinsic substantial nature. Why is this so?
Because the entities of those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are all substantially real.
If the essence of the aggregates and so forth were truly non-existent,
the Blessed One would not have taught the specific and general characteristics of the great elements and other phenomena;
furthermore, if dharmas such as form were like the horns of a rabbit, [they would be utterly non-existent].
If it is argued that things do not truly exist and there is only consciousness,
then it would be unreasonable for internal mind to manifest phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) when they were originally non-existent,
because phenomena such as form cannot arise without a cause.
Furthermore, if the mind could manifest without a cause,
then things such as tortoise hair, rabbit horns, and the son of a barren woman should also be obtainable.
Moreover, this is because it refutes external objects.
Furthermore, if one analyzes gross phenomena down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*),
and since those ultimate atoms possess spatial dimensions and thus lack substantial reality, it is illogical to claim that "there is only consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*).
When the various preceding and succeeding parts of the consciousness-mind are analyzed,
they are not established as being substantially existent and identical;
therefore, one should not make such a statement.
"There is only internal mind and no external objects.
Furthermore, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught the two types of phenomena— internal and external dependent origination and dependent nature— separately,
both the mind and external objects truly exist.
As for those passages in various sūtras that state there are no external objects and only consciousness-mind,
they were spoken in this way because [the Buddha] wished to refute views such as eternalism.
The philosophical tenets of the Madhyamaka school are the same as those of the Hīnayāna.
Since these two are combined and collectively termed "Hīnayāna," they are not discussed separately.
Other instances of establishing [positions] and refuting [opponents] follow.
The details are not recounted here for fear of excessive prolixity.
Regarding the Mahāyāna schools, there are likewise three distinctions.
The first is the school based on the sūtras.
It is also called the "Ultimate Truth School," which takes emptiness as its primary tenet;
it is also known as the "School that Refutes Characteristics.
Second is the "Middle Way School of Consciousness-Only."
It is also called the School of Rational and Perfect Reality (Yingli Yuanshi Zong),
and it is also termed the School that Establishes Characteristics (Lixiang Zong).
Third is the Middle School based on the Treatises (Yilun Zhongzhong).
It is also called the School of the Perfect Interfusion of Dharmatā,
and is also termed the Dharmatā School.
Regarding the statement "the school based on the sūtras":
Six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
various sectarian schools arose in competition;
most became attached to views of existence.
He slandered the Mahāyāna Dharma and destroyed the True Teaching in the kingdom of South India.
There was a bodhisattva who appeared in the world,
named Nāgārjuna.
Having realized the Ground of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),
in order to refute the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*),
he composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other treatises based on Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Later, his disciples, such as the noble Āryadeva and others among the great dialecticians,
also composed works such as the *Śataśāstra*,
extensively elucidating the great meaning.
Therefore, based on this, there arises this school and this view:
how is it that the three natures of non-existence are taken as the definitive meaning?
It is taught that all phenomena exist conventionally,
yet are empty from the perspective of ultimate truth.
This means that because all phenomena exist through dependent origination,
they are termed "conventional.
Furthermore, because that very dependent origination is empty of intrinsic nature, it is [the ultimate].
Therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The ultimate truth and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) do not differ in essence.
Because their essence does not differ, they are neither empty nor existent; this "neither empty nor existent" is the Middle Way principle.
Because one attains the Middle Way, one does not abide in the two extremes.

Although there is that which is eliminated based on conventional truth, through the cultivation of observing ultimate truth, there is nothing to be apprehended; as calm abiding and insight proceed in tandem, the path of non-abiding is accomplished.
Based on conventional truth, the three natures are taught;
however, from the perspective of ultimate truth, all three natures of non-existence are absent.
It is by grasping at the conventional that saṃsāra is spoken of.
Because it brings about liberation, the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) is taught;
therefore, there is no designation of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
Regarding this definitive meaning (nītārtha), there is further establishment and refutation.
The details are not recounted here for fear of prolixity.
As for the term "the central tenet of Vijñaptimātra," it is so called because the aforementioned preceding tenets have already arisen.
Consequently, sentient beings again became attached to the view of emptiness.
Nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga appeared in the world;
he had attained the first bhūmi and achieved the meditative concentration of the Light of Dharma (dharmāloka-samādhi).
In order to refute the view of emptiness, he composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga had a younger half-brother named Vasubandhu.
He advanced in rank and practice,
and also composed the *Triṃśikā-śāstra* and other treatises, establishing the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Therefore, this school arises.
What is the view of this school?
It holds that external phenomena such as form do not exist in reality.
In the manifestation of consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra),
all that is spoken of in the world and in treatises as the self and various phenomena is merely the internal consciousness transforming and appearing as external objects.
Due to the power of the habitual tendencies of the discrimination between self and phenomena,
when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as if they were self and phenomena;
although these appearances of self and phenomena exist within internal consciousness, [they are perceived as external].
However, through conceptual construction, these appear as if they were external objects.
Since beginningless time, sentient beings have taken these as real selves and real phenomena;
therefore, one should know that no such objects exist.
Why is this so? Because we directly perceive that coarse forms are composed of an accumulation of subtle atoms,
and yet those atoms possess six spatial dimensions.
Because those [objects] are not established, external objects do not exist.
It is like one with cataracts seeing falling hairs in empty space.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
The supreme sons of the Victorious Ones [declare that] the three realms are mind-only.
Furthermore, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states:
"All things, both internal and external..."
What is perceived is nothing but one's own mind;
the minds of sentient beings possess a dual nature:
the grasper and the grasped.
The essence of mind has two gates;
thus, the mind perceives two objects.
Ordinary beings are deluded by their own nature.
Because one cannot comprehend this for oneself,
one should know that external objects do not exist and that it is only consciousness that manifests.
Furthermore, that conscious mind arises in a constant succession.

When the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is truly attained, there likewise exists the non-dual correct cognition that is free from the grasping subject; it is truly existent and not non-existent.
Furthermore, the teaching on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) is established as a definitive exposition of ultimate meaning (*nītārtha*).
All phenomena, by virtue of the two truths, are neither empty nor existent.
Among the three natures,
the nature of the thoroughly imagined is entirely non-existent.
The dependent nature exists conventionally through causes and conditions;
the perfected nature is the reality free from delusion,
as that which is grasped does not exist.
It is empty yet not non-existent,
for it exists in dependence upon the perfected nature;
it is existent yet not empty.
Neither existent nor empty—
this is the principle therein.

Due to delusion regarding the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), one forms attachments to the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) within the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), [conceiving] either a self or dharmas.

Through the vision of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one awakens to the knowledge that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is like an illusion and not real, thereby becoming free from this grasping.

Thus, one knows that the dependent and perfected natures definitely exist; it is for the sake of dispelling such grasping that the three natures of non-existence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) are taught, and not because the other [natures] do not exist.
Because their nature is entirely non-existent, the three natures are said to be the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Other positions, along with their refutations and proofs,
are as explained in treatises such as the *Viṃśatikā* and the *Triṃśikā*.
Regarding the "central tenet" (madhyamaka) mentioned in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
it is said that the Bodhisattva Asaṅga had a disciple named Nandaśrīta.
Based on the treatises such as the *Madhyamakālaṃkāra* composed by Asaṅga,
they establish that conventional phenomena are identical to the Yogācāra school; yet, regarding the ultimate truth,
they are identical to the Madhyamaka in that all things are empty of intrinsic nature.
Why is this so? If there were objects existing externally apart from consciousness and mind,
it would not be logical.
When consciousness cognizes an object,
it is able to discern it because the external object is the very nature of that consciousness.
If it were not thus, one could not achieve clear understanding.
Furthermore, it would be unreasonable to claim that this conscious mind exists as a reality.
Because external forms and so forth are of the nature of consciousness,
just as external objects possess various names, seeds,
and characteristics, the mind likewise possesses many such varieties.
Furthermore, just as consciousness has no form, external objects are likewise invisible;
therefore, one should know that these two faults exist,
and [external objects] do not truly exist.
Furthermore, there are other positions established as explained elsewhere;
despite such differences in tenets and views, [the following remains].
Now, in explaining this sūtra,
one should reflect upon it according to reason solely based on the tenets set forth within the sūtra itself.
Having completed the establishment of the tenets:
Second, regarding the "returning to the vehicle":
if one discusses the essence of the Dharma,
there is no establishment of vehicles.
Because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ,
he guides them according to their individual dispositions;
thus, he provisionally speaks of many types.
Although there are many types of seeds,
to speak briefly,
they do not exceed three kinds.
First, the Śrāvaka vehicle;
second, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and third, the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Regarding the term "Śrāvaka-yāna" (the Vehicle of the Hearers):
they are called Śrāvakas because they awaken to the Way through sound and thereby attain thorough penetration.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
Regarding the term "śrāvaka" (disciple):
it refers to one who, having heard from a virtuous friend, realizes the fruit for themselves and enables others to hear it as well.
Therefore, they are called śrāvakas.
As for the term "vehicle" (yāna),
it carries the meaning of "transporting" or "carrying across."
As will be explained below,
the cultivation and realization of this vehicle are for those of inferior faculties.
Among the Four Noble Truths,
one first realizes that these five aggregates of clinging are tainted.
Knowing this to be the locus upon which all suffering depends,
and perceiving it as coarse and easy to observe,
one immediately awakens to the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
Furthermore, by investigating the cause of suffering, one is able to understand that it is karma and afflictions;
this is called awakening to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
By abandoning karma and afflictions, one becomes detached from the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
To fully understand peace and happiness is to realize the Truth of Cessation; to fully understand the Eightfold Noble Path is to realize the means for that cessation.
This is what is called awakening to the Truth of the Path.
Thus, these contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena consist solely of cause and effect;
herein, there is no agent and no life-principle.
Seeing in this way, one realizes the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Furthermore, one can discern that birth and death are extreme suffering while nirvāṇa is pure and sublime;
thus, regarding these two phenomena, one abandons the former and adopts the latter.
Averse to and fearful of birth and death, their compassion and wisdom are extremely deficient;
they practice all wholesome dharmas such as the six perfections not for the sake of many, but solely for their own bodies.
When attaining the realization of the direct vision of the bliss of nirvāṇa,
if one lacks virtuous friends,
one cannot personally awaken to the true nature of the Four Noble Truths.
Because their faculties are dull,
it is called the "inferior vehicle" (hīnayāna).
As for what is called the "Pratyekabuddha Vehicle":
Because they possess middling faculties,
they enter through the gateway of the twelve links of dependent origination to thoroughly understand that old age and death are the defects of birth and death,
and they subsequently seek their cause.
From birth onwards, there is such a reverse investigation leading back to ignorance; thus,
the ear serves as both cause and effect.
There is only dependent origination and the nature of conditions;
one realizes the selflessness of persons through the absence of "self" and "mine.
Furthermore, one understands that from the cessation of ignorance up to old age and death, nothing arises.
Thus, one is able to thoroughly understand dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena in both their forward and reverse orders, as well as their defiled and purified aspects;
consequently, one comes to feel revulsion toward birth and death,
while joyfully seeking the pure and sublime.
Because their compassion and wisdom are inferior, all the wholesome dharmas they cultivate, such as the six perfections,
are practiced solely for their own benefit and do not benefit the multitude;
therefore, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding those who speak of the Bodhisattva Vehicle:
because their faculties are superior,
they contemplate all phenomena within the perspective of ultimate truth.
Fundamentally, it is empty and quiescent;
birth-and-death and nirvana are utterly without dual characteristics.
This is according to the conventional truth.
Realizing all things to be like illusions,
they possess the wisdom of great compassion and do not abandon saṃsāra.
Without grasping at nirvāṇa,
they cultivate the ten perfections and so forth for the sake of all sentient beings.
Having fulfilled the benefit of oneself and others,
one who knows the stages and the realization of the fruit through essential terms is called a follower of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
There are seven great meanings that surpass the Two Vehicles,
as explained below.
Now, within this sutra, it is subsumed under the Bodhisattvayāna,
for it is not an object of focus for the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha).
This concludes the clarification of the refuge in the vehicle.
Third, regarding the classification into three categories:
although all the holy teachings are immeasurable,
they are grouped according to their common characteristics.
There are twelve divisions,
namely:
the Sūtras.
Geya (Verses),
Vyākaraṇa (Prophecies),
and Gāthā (Stanzas).
Discourses spoken by the Buddha himself (udāna), discourses on dependent origination (nidāna),
and discourses using parables (avadāna).
Itivṛttaka, Jātaka,
and Vaipulya.
It is truly marvelous!
This is the *Dharmaparyāya-sūtra*.
As for what is called a "Sūtra":
This refers to the sense of "pervading.
In the prose, it directly explains the various categories and the essential nature of the underlying intentions.
As for the term "verses" (geya):
This refers to the proclamation of verses (gāthā) following prose passages;
furthermore, it refers to the brief indication of those sūtras of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
As for "prophecies" (vyākaraṇa):
This refers to the detailed analysis of the meaning briefly indicated [in the preceding section], as well as the recording of the rebirth places of deceased disciples.
As for "verses" (*geya*),
they are recorded by means of metrical lines (*pāda*).
It may be spoken in two lines, or in three, four, five, or six lines.
As for "spoken of one's own accord" (svayambhāṣita),
this refers to speaking without being requested.
It is for the sake of causing disciples to attain resolute conviction,
and for the sake of causing superior beings among those to be converted to abide in the supreme principle that he speaks spontaneously.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The World-Honored One now spontaneously proclaims this.
As for what is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda),
it refers to that which is taught in response to a request.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"At one time, the Blessed One, relying on the case of the black *karkaṭaka* fruit, expounded the essential points of the Dharma for the bhikṣus," and so forth.
Regarding the term "illustrative example" (*dṛṣṭānta*):
This refers to the *Avadāna-sūtras*,
by which hidden meanings become clear through the use of analogies.
As for the term "Itivṛttaka" (Past Events):
This refers to all matters concerning the past that are proclaimed, excluding the Jātaka tales.
As for "Jātaka," it refers to the proclamation of one's own former births while practicing the bodhisattva path in past lives.
Regarding the term "Vaipulya" (Extensive Teachings):
it refers to the exposition of the bodhisattva path and the proclamation of the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*),
namely, the four kinds of universal purity up to the supreme wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākāra-jñatā*).
Regarding the term "unprecedented phenomena" (adbhuta-dharma):
this refers to the marvelous teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas, the Śrāvakas, or lay practitioners,
as found in various sūtras.
Discourse arises from rare and extraordinary matters.
What is called "discursive discussion" refers to the various sūtras, vinayas, and abhidharmas.
Thus, all sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha) are called mātṛkā and are also termed abhidharma.
This present sūtra is included within the section on self-explanations and discourses among the twelvefold division of the teachings.
The explanation of the classification into twelve divisions is concluded.
Fourth, regarding the discourse on the *Guīzàng* (Treasury of Return):
these twelve divisions of the teaching are collectively subsumed into three.
First is the Sūtra Piṭaka,
here translated as "Scripture" (Kīng).
It threads together and connects the teachings on the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
Because it accords with the principle and accords with the capacity [of beings], it gathers and benefits others;
thus, "pitaka" (藏) means "to gather.
Second is the Vinaya-piṭaka, which here is translated as "Discipline" (調伏).
The training in ethical discipline that is thus encompassed harmonizes the three types of action and subdues unwholesome conduct.
And because it encompasses and benefits [beings],
there is the third Piṭaka, the Abhidharma-kośa;
this is translated here as "Abhidharma" (the Higher Dharma).
The wisdom training (*prajñā-śikṣā*) is that which is to be fully explained,
for it benefits by being directed toward *nirvāṇa* and by contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
How do these three [trainings] subsume the twelve [links]?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The twelvefold division of the teaching thus described is subsumed within the three baskets (*piṭaka*).
It should be understood that among these, when the sūtras are mentioned..."
Geya (Verses),
Vyākaraṇa (Prophecies),
and Gāthā (Stanzas).
Itivuttaka (Sayings),
Jātaka (Birth Stories),
and Vetullaka (Past Deeds).
Jātaka, Vaipulya,
and Adbhutadharma— these are called the Sūtra Piṭaka.
If it speaks of causes and conditions, it is called the Vinaya Piṭaka;
if it speaks of formal expositions, it is called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Therefore, these twelve divisions of the teaching are subsumed within the three piṭakas.
Furthermore, the Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya states:
"Thus, it is comprised within the three collections of the sūtras and so forth;
namely, the sūtra."
Geya, Vyākaraṇa, and Gāthā.
These are the self-explanations;
they all belong to the Sūtra Piṭaka of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
This is the Dependent Origination.
Parables (avadāna),
past events (itivṛttaka),
and birth stories (jātaka).
Together with their associated retinues, these are called the Vinaya Piṭaka;
as well as the Vaipulya and the Adbhutadharma.
This is the Bodhisattva Piṭaka of Sūtras;
as for the discourses on the treatises (śāstra),
they constitute those two Piṭakas of Abhidharma.
For what reason did the Tathāgata establish the Three Piṭakas?
To counteract the secondary affliction of doubt, he established the Sūtra Piṭaka;
to counteract the secondary afflictions of falling into the two extremes, he established the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Abhidharma Piṭaka was taught as an antidote to the secondary affliction of adherence to views;
this present sutra is included within that Abhidharma Piṭaka.
The explanation of the Piṭakas is concluded.
Fifth, regarding the explanation:
the main section of the sutra is divided into two parts.
First is the explanation of the title.
The second part explains the main text.
This first section is further divided into three parts.
The first is the explanation of the meaning of "Mahāyāna."
Second, the explanation of the "rice seedling" (śālistamba);
third, the explanation of the meaning of the sūtra.
Regarding the first point, concerning the term "Mahāyāna":
It is called "Great" because it surpasses the two vehicles by way of seven kinds of greatness.
Regarding these seven kinds of greatness:
first is the greatness of the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Second, the greatness of generating the mind; third, the greatness of great faith and joy;
fourth, the greatness of reflection;
fifth, the greatness of the provisions.
Sixth is greatness of time;
seventh is greatness of accomplishment.
Regarding "greatness of the object":
This is as taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Mahāsannipāta*, the *Mahāratnakūṭa*, and other sūtras,
because all phenomena are the objects of focus for bodhisattvas. Thus,
it is said that the "greatness" of generating the mind [of enlightenment] consists in this.
It is for the sake of generating the unsurpassed bodhicitta that one is said to "rely with faith on the great";
it is for the sake of relying with faith on the profoundly deep Dharma.
Regarding "greatness of reflection," it refers to reflecting for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Regarding "greatness of the provisions," it refers to...
Because it possesses the two great merits of merit and wisdom,
it is called "great in time," as it proceeds toward enlightenment for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the great," it refers to the accomplishment of various great virtues such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
As for the term "vehicle" (*yāna*), its meaning is that of "carrying across."

It is like a boat or raft that carries sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death, enabling them to reach the further shore of nirvāṇa. Second, regarding the term "rice sprout" (*śālistamba*):
all sūtras establish their titles based on four meanings.
What are the four?
First, the location;
second, the person.
There are three dharmas and four similes.
Regarding the term "place" (sthāna):
Regarding those that establish names based on the person, such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and others; regarding those that establish names based on the teaching,
such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and others.
Regarding names established from the Dharma,
examples include the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and others.
Regarding names established from metaphors:
As stated in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
when that sūtra was being preached,
bodhisattvas from the ten directions...
For example, it is called the "Jewel Cloud" because great clouds gather together;
this sutra is likewise so named because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached this Dharma after observing the rice seedlings. Third, as for the term "sutra":
The explanations found in various sūtras and śāstras follow many paths;
here, I shall briefly cite two meanings.
The first is the meaning of permanence.
It is called "constant" (*nitya*) because it does not change throughout the past and present;

second, it is called "essential" (*sāra*) because it universally encompasses all phenomena. Regarding the second point, the explanation of the main text, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its section on "Exegesis" (*Vyākhyāna-bhūmi*), states:
Now, one who wishes to explain all sutras should provide a general explanation of those sutras by means of five gates.
What are these five?
First, the gate of general inclusion;
second, that which is elucidated by the sūtra;
third, the explanation of the meaning of the phrases.
Fourth is the sequence of the four analytical knowledges;
fifth is the resolution of objections.
This sutra is likewise so.
This is also analyzed and discerned through five divisions; within the first section, it is further divided into seven:

From the time the Venerable Śāriputra spoke these words until the conclusion of the sutra,

The first eight are afflictions;

The twelve [links] are subsumed within three.
The Sūtra proceeds from Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s reply to the Venerable Śāriputra, up to: "In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering."
This is the Dharma of dependent origination taught by the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of what is to be known":
it is because this path is able to know the nature of all phenomena.
The eightfold noble path is called the nature of that which is to be known (*jñeya*).
From the sutra passage "What is the Dharma? up to "this is the eightfold noble path," five phrases refer to the fruit of that which is to be known.

This is because the sutra proceeds from the fruit and nirvana down to the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training.

As the Sūtra asks: "How does one see dependent origination as taught by the Buddha?"
Therefore, one should contemplate the dharma of causes and conditions through five aspects.
What is essential in the seven-syllable verses is this:
namely, the removal of the two kinds of obstacles and the attainment of the path to non-abiding nirvana.
If one were to discuss the principles of non-abiding nirvana, they are immeasurable;
yet, to speak briefly, there are two kinds. What are these two?
This refers to the two qualities of compassion and wisdom possessed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

What is called the cognitive hindrance refers to...

The section from "The Sūtra by means of the Venerable Śāriputra" up to "faithfully receiving and practicing" concludes the General Summary Gate. Regarding the second major gate, as for that which is elucidated by the Sūtra:

Question:
For what reason do the compilers of the sūtras not say "Spoken by [the Buddha] himself," but rather say, "Thus have I heard"?
Answer:
It is said "I heard" in order to avoid the slanders of exaggeration and depreciation.
These two [terms] indicate that [the teaching] was heard directly from [the Buddha] and was not personally realized;
the term "I" is established so as to show that it was heard directly by oneself,
thereby avoiding the fault of being hearsay.
Because hearing alone is not a realization,
"hearing" is established;
this excludes the Buddha alone.
Others, however, cannot comprehend this meaning;
if it is argued that self-realization does not produce conviction,
[the text] speaks of "at one time."
This refers to the time when one hears the sutra.
There are two interpretations of this:
first, it accords with the characteristic of hearing.
Second, it is conjoined with abiding.
Regarding its conjunction with hearing:
this reveals that this jewel of a sutra is difficult to hear.
Regarding "conjoined with abiding":
this indicates that the Tathāgata, at other times, dwells in other places for the sake of delivering sentient beings.

Bhagavān; this is the accomplishment of these two Lords.

the shape and appearance of this mountain's peaks resemble those of a vulture.

This sutra is likewise so.

This reveals the meaning of supreme excellence.

First, because he never departs from the Buddha among all the śrāvakas and constantly serves as his attendant;

The reason he taught this Dharma to the bhikṣus was his desire to lead those of lesser capacity toward the Great Dharma.
Why did the World-Honored One remain silent after teaching the Dharma?
If one were to discuss the sagely intent, it is subtle and difficult to fathom;
nevertheless, according to inference (*anumāna*), there are three points of meaning.
The first is for the purpose of eliminating pride.
First, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he constantly forms this thought:
"Although the Buddha has spoken but little, I am able to realize the Great [Vehicle]"; it is in order to remove this pride.
Second, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he is able to explain the Tathāgata’s secret intentions and praise their virtues.
Third, because this is complete and lacks nothing else.
Regarding the term "Sugata":

Those who have passed away depart;
having departed, they do not return.
Therefore, he is named Sugata, the Well-Gone One.
As for what those matters are:
the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma does not depart from four kinds of cryptic expressions and four kinds of underlying intentions.
Among these eight points:

because one wishes to lead those inclined toward the Lesser Vehicle into the Great Vehicle and its fruits,
the aggregates, elements, and so forth are taught.

for the sake of counteracting the eighty-four thousand afflictions through the Abhidharma,

as stated in the Abhidharma treatises:
"Perceiving the non-solid as solid, one dwells well within inversion."
Though afflicted by the utmost afflictions, one attains the unsurpassed path.

the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) according to a distinct meaning is as follows:

Question:

What is called "causes and conditions" refers to the causes and effects associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is called "Dharma" refers to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and unconditioned nirvana (*asaṃskṛta-nirvāṇa*).
What is called "Buddha" refers to the untainted fruits, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
These natures and characteristics are each dissimilar. How can one,
by perceiving such dissimilar causes and conditions,
perceive the Dharma-Buddha?
If one were able to see, the eye would also hear sounds and so forth;
because there is this doubt, the question is posed.
[From] the Sūtra.

"What is the causal condition? What is the Dharma? What is the Buddha? How is it that by seeing the causal condition one can see the Dharma? And how is it that by seeing the Dharma one can see the Buddha? Having spoken these words, these are the five inquiries.

This is the initial heading.

For what reason are exactly twelve factors enumerated?
Answer: It is for five reasons.

Second are the projected factors,
namely name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
Third are the actualizing factors.
Craving, grasping, and becoming are the four factors that constitute [the cause];
birth is [the result].
The five factors of affliction are old age and death.
The projecting factors are the remote causes.
That which is capable of accomplishing the factors is the proximate cause;
for if these two were absent, birth would not be established.
Therefore, two causes are taught.
By these five meanings, if there were fewer than twelve, the requirements would not be complete;

Question:
Question: Since you do not state a cause for ignorance (*avidyā*), does this not imply that saṃsāra has a beginning, and that ignorance arises without a cause? Answer:
Because ignorance has arisen based on its own nature (*svabhāva*) and conditions (*pratyaya*) from time immemorial, it has no beginning; thus, it is not established as being without a cause.
If it is argued that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is not the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*),
this is not a correct reason because it is merely a contributory condition (*sahakāri-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, since improper mental attention and the like are themselves of the nature of ignorance, there is no contradiction with reason.
Sūtra:
"In this way, there arises only a mass of pure and extreme suffering. These are the three fetters.
The word "only" (kevala) is used because they are devoid of self and what belongs to self.

There are two kinds of negation:
first, the negation of non-existence;
second, the negation of what is not [that].
This is because it excludes what is not [the case].
For example, it is like a person whose eyes have been treated with the elixir of immortality;
this is also like that.

Because, through the power of cultivating the path, one does not associate with ignorance and the like, but attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and causes it to gradually increase and become superior;
therefore, the cessation of ignorance and so forth is also called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the teaching of the two kinds of dependently arisen phenomena:

Sūtra.
"In this way, there is only the cessation of this entire mass of pure and extreme suffering"— this is the second [point], the connection.

"What is this Dharma? This is the first [section].
The meaning of the text is clear. The Sūtra states:

"That which is called the eight factors of the noble path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. These are the two answers.
If one discusses the Dharma, there are three types.
What is being explained here refers to the Dharma of practice,
for these Eightfold Noble Paths constitute the Dharma of practice.
To possess non-erroneous vision regarding the principle of reality as it is is called right view.
To deliberate according to reason is called right intention.
To speak in accordance with reality is [right speech].
To be free from verbal transgressions and for one's vocal karma to be pure is called right speech.
Being free from the three qualities of the body and having purity of bodily action is called right action.
Abstaining from the four types of wrong livelihood and seeking [sustenance] in accordance with the Dharma so that body and speech are pure is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
One cultivates valor in order to eliminate other obstacles, faults, and evils.
It is called right effort.
To clearly remember and not forget the object of focus is called right mindfulness.
To focus the mind on a single object in order to seek superior qualities is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
These eight branches of the Noble Path are thus comprised of six factors.
First is the factor of discernment,

The second is the branch of manifestation,

Third is the limb of faithful acceptance,

The fourth is the limb of removing obstacles: because one does not perform unwholesome actions and maintains purity of precepts;

Just as sprouts arise from seeds, so too do flowers and fruits arise; these three constitute the proof.
This demonstrates the meaning of that which is established.
Second, the section clarifying arising from causes that lack a creator.
The text has four parts:
first, clarifying that the cause has no agent;
second, [clarifying] that the fruit has no agent.
Third, although there is no agent, the fruit is produced; this concludes the fourth section of the sutra.

It states: "That seed does not form the thought, 'I can produce the sprout,' nor does the sprout form the thought, 'I am produced from the seed,' and so on until the flower does not form the thought, 'I can produce the fruit,' nor does the fruit form the thought, 'I am produced from the flower. This first and second [point] clarifies that both the cause and the fruit lack an agent.
This demonstrates that there is only a cause and no agent.
If the various agents were the causes [of phenomena],
they would have no connection with those phenomena.
Because it is not beneficial [to the seed]. Sūtra:

"Nevertheless, because the seed exists, the sprout is able to arise; likewise, because the flower exists, the fruit is thereby able to be accomplished. These three [examples] show that although there is no agent, the fruit is produced.
Since this is already evident in the scriptural text, it is not explained here. The scripture states:
"One should contemplate the meaning of the causal correspondence of external dependent origination in this way. These are the four conclusions.
The concluding passage is evident.
Next, the second section, the correspondence of conditions,
is explained in three parts.
First, from the perspective of arising through conditions that are capable of producing;
second, from the perspective of arising through conditions that lack an agent;
and finally, by refuting erroneous views.
The first part is further divided into seven sections:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
Third, the inquiry;
fourth, the response enumerating the items;
fifth, the conclusion.
Sixth, the clarification of functional activity;
seventh, the scriptural proof.
"How should one contemplate the meaning of the correspondence of conditions in external dependent origination? This is the first question.
The Sūtra says:
"It is because of the conjunction of the six elements."
These two are the answers.
The sūtra asks:
"By the conjunction of which six elements? These three are the inquiries.
The Sūtra states:

"That which arises through the combination of external causes and conditions, such as the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, and direction. These four answers enumerate the categories.
The essential meaning of the six elements is as follows in the sutra text:
"One should contemplate the external dependent origination in terms of the principle of the correspondence of conditions. These are the five fetters.

The Sūtra states: "The earth element can support the seed; the water element moistens the seed; the fire element warms the seed; the wind element moves the seed; the space element does not obstruct the seed; and time can transform the seed. These six clarify their functional activities.
That which is called the earth element has solidity as its nature;
the water element has fluidity and moisture as its nature.
The fire element has heat and dryness as its nature;
the wind element has lightness and mobility as its nature;
and the space-wind [element] has vacuity and pervasion as its nature.
This, moreover, is twofold:
namely, light and darkness.
As for "time," it is established in reference to the four great elements, such as earth and so forth.
Sūtra:

"If these various conditions are absent, the seed cannot produce a sprout; if the external earth element is present and all others are likewise complete—extending thus to water, fire, wind, space, time, and so forth—and if everything is fully assembled, then at the moment the seed ceases, the sprout is produced. This is the seventh proof.
The scriptural passage is visible [in the source].
Second, the section clarifying the gate of arising from conditions that lack an agent has six parts.
First, the absence of an agent in conditions;
second, the absence of an agent in causes;
third, the absence of an agent in effects.
Fourth, although there is no agent, its fruit is accomplished;
fifth, the proof;
sixth, the conclusion.

Sūtra: In this regard, the earth element does not form the thought, "I am able to support the seed"; likewise, the water element does not form the thought, "I am able to moisten the seed"; the fire element does not form the thought, "I am able to warm the seed"; the wind element does not form the thought, "I am able to cause the seed to move"; the space element does not form the thought, "I am able to provide non-obstruction for the seed"; and the season does not form the thought, "I am able to transform the seed. This first section clarifies that among the six conditions, there is no agent.
Sūtra:
Furthermore, the seed does not form the thought, "I am able to produce the sprout. These two causes are devoid of an agent.
Sūtra.
The sprout, too, does not form the thought: "I am now arising from these various conditions. These three illustrate that the fruit has no agent. As the Sūtra says:

"Nevertheless, although these various conditions exist, when the seed perishes, the sprout immediately arises; likewise, when there is the flower, the fruit immediately arises. Thus, although these four have no agent, they bring their fruit to completion.
Sūtra:

That sprout is not produced by itself, nor produced by another, nor produced by both self and other, nor produced by Īśvara, nor transformed by time, nor born of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor arisen without cause. Nevertheless, when the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time converge and the seed perishes, the sprout is produced. These are the five proofs that establish [this point].
Regarding the statement that they are not self-made:
whether the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena exists or does not exist,
it cannot be established because it does not act as its own cause and lacks any functional activity.
Speech, moreover, is not created by another;
for there is no creator who first conceives an intention and then performs the act.
This demonstrates that all phenomena (dharmas) are without self (anātman).
It is said that [phenomena] are not created by both self and other because they are neither produced by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor by anything else.
It is said that they are not created by Īśvara,
for he would be the cause of all phenomena, being eternally sovereign and producing them from time to time.
This contradicts reason,
because the causes are fully present.
Furthermore, it is not the case that [the nature] changes over time.
Because all phenomena exist through provisional causes and conditions and do not depend on time,
it is said that they do not arise from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
this is because they are not phenomena as conceived by the Sāṃkhya school.
This, then, eliminates the cause of dissimilarity.
As for the statement that "it is also not produced without a cause," it is because all phenomena arise through provisional causes and conditions.
This is the view that [the world] arises without cause.
The Sūtra says:
"Therefore, one should contemplate the meaning of the correspondence of conditions in external dependent origination in this way. These are the six fetters.
The three knowledges (vidyā) refute wrong views.
This section has five parts;
the first is the heading.
First, the question; second, the answer;
third, the response;
fourth, the explanation.
V. Summary. Sūtra:
"One should contemplate those external dependent origination factors by means of five aspects. This is the initial heading.
[Sūtra]:
What are the five? These are the two questions.
[Sūtra].
"Not eternal, not annihilated, not transmigrating; from a small cause, a great fruit arises that resembles it"—these are the three answers.
"How is it not eternal? up to "therefore it resembles it"—this is the fourfold explanation.
The text has five parts:
first, clarifying that [phenomena] are not eternal;
second, clarifying that they are not annihilated.
Third, the three types of knowledge do not shift.
Fourth, from a small cause, a great result arises.
Fifth, there is similarity.
The first part is further divided into three sections:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
The Sūtra on the Three Fetters asks:
"What is non-eternalism? This is the first question.
The Sūtra states:

"Because the sprout and the seed are distinct from one another, that sprout is not the seed; yet the sprout arises neither when the seed has been destroyed nor when it has not ceased. It is at the time the seed is destroyed that the sprout arises. These are the two answers.
If these were permanent, it could not be said that "this is the cause" and "this is the fruit.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "For this reason, these three fetters are not permanent. Second, the explanation of non-cessation.
The text has three parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
The subsequent conclusion.
The Sūtra says:
"What is non-interruption? This is the first question.
The Sūtra states:

"The sprout does not arise from a past seed that has perished, nor does it arise without the seed having ceased; rather, at the very moment the seed perishes, the sprout arises, like the rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. These are the two answers.
Because the continuity of cause and effect is without interruption,
it is called "uninterrupted.
This can be seen in the preceding text.
Sūtra:
For this reason, these three fetters are not severed;
the three knowledges do not shift.
The text has three parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
The subsequent conclusion.
The Sūtra asks:
"How is it that there is no shifting? This is the first question.
The Sūtra states:
"The sprout is distinct from the seed, for the sprout is not the seed. These are the two answers.
Because the cause is distinct from the seed, it is called "non-transference."
Sūtra:
Therefore, these three fetters do not shift.
Fourth, it clarifies how small causes produce great results.
The text has three parts:
first, the question;
second, the answer.
The subsequent conclusion.
The Sūtra says:
"How can a small cause produce a great fruit? This is the first question.
Sūtra:
"From a small seed, a great fruit arises. These are the two answers, such as the case of the *kovidāra* tree and others.
Although the stem and leaves are extremely small, they are very large;
thus, a great fruit arises from a small cause.
Sūtra.
Therefore, from a small cause a great fruit arises; these are the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The fifth [section] is on "Similarity" (*sādharmya*), which consists of three parts.
First the question,
next the answer,
and finally the conclusion.
Sūtra:
"In what way is it similar to that? This is the first question.
Sūtra:
Because the fruit arises from the seed that was planted; these are the two answers.
It is like a rice seed, which produces its own corresponding fruit.
It is not for any other purpose,
but for the sake of the fruit and the cause,
because it is non-perverted.
This demonstrates that there is no loss of karmic function.
There are two kinds of factors by which karmic function is lost: first, [the presence of] equality and smallness; second, the production of results from inverted conditions.
Sūtra.
Therefore, they are similar to those; these are the three fetters (*saṃyojana*). Sūtra:
Thus, one contemplates the dharma of external conditions in five ways; these are the five summary points.
The concluding passage is evident.
This completes the explanation of external dependent origination. Second is the explanation of internal dependent origination.
The text is divided into two parts.
First, correspondence with causes;
second, correspondence with conditions.
The first is further divided into three.
1. The gate of arising from various causes of impermanence;
2. The gate of arising from the causes that are capable of producing;
3. The gate of arising from causes that lack an agent.
Sūtra:

"Thus, regarding this internal dependent origination, it extends to what is called 'correspondence with causes' and 'correspondence with conditions. This first section clarifies the gateway of arising from various impermanent causes.
The text has three parts:
first, the heading;
second, the question.
The subsequent answer in the Sūtra states:
"In this way, the internal dependent origination also arises by means of two kinds. This is the initial heading.
Sūtra: What are the two? These are the two questions. Sūtra.
That which is called "correspondence with causes" and "correspondence with conditions"—these are the three answers.
Second, the section clarifying the gate of arising from the productive cause;
this text has three parts.
First the question,
next the answer,
and finally the proof.
Sūtra:
What is the meaning of the causal correspondence of the internal dependent origination? This is the first question.
Sūtra:
That which is called "beginning from ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, up to birth as the condition for aging and death" constitutes the second answer.

The Sūtra states: "If ignorance does not arise, volitional formations will not exist; ... up to ... if birth does not exist, aging and death will not exist. Thus, because there is ignorance, volitional formations come to be; ... up to ... because there is birth, aging and death come to be. This constitutes the third proof.
The three knowledges arise from the gate of causes that lack an agent;
furthermore, there are four [points],
the first of which is that the cause lacks an agent.
Second, the fruit has no agent;
third, although there is no agent, its fruit is nevertheless accomplished;
fourth, the conclusion.
The Sūtra states:

"Ignorance does not form the thought, 'I am able to produce volitional formations,' nor do volitional formations form the thought, 'I have arisen from ignorance. ... [and so on] until: birth does not form the thought, 'I am able to produce old age and death,' nor does old age and death form the thought, 'I have arisen from birth. This pair of points clarifies that there is no agent in the cause and no agent in the fruit.
This can be seen in the sūtra:
"Although there is ignorance, formations arise; likewise, because there is birth, old age and death come to be. Thus, although these three lack an agent, their results are nonetheless accomplished.
Sūtra:
Therefore, one should contemplate the meaning of the causal correspondence of internal dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in this way. These are the four conclusions.
Second, the explanation of the meaning of the conditional correspondence (*pratyaya-saṃprayoga*) consists of eight sections.
First, the gate of arising from various impermanent causes;
second, the gate of arising from conditioning factors that bring about accomplishment;
third, the gate of arising from conditions devoid of an agent.
Fourth, the discernment of the essence;
fifth, the explanation of the names;
sixth, the continuity of the branches.
Seventh, the departure from the two extremes;
eighth, the gathering of causes.
The first section is divided into five parts.
First, the question;
second, the answer;
third, the inquiry.
Fourth, the enumeration of the items in response;
fifth, the conclusion. Sūtra.
"How should one contemplate the phenomena associated with conditions within the internal law of dependent origination? This is the first question.
"Because of the conjunction of the six elements. This is the second answer.
Sūtra:
By what six elements is there a combination? These are the three inquiries.
Sūtra.
That which is called the "conjunction of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness" refers to the enumeration of these four [elements] as listed in the Sūtra.
"One should contemplate the internal dependent origination and the phenomena associated with its conditions" concludes these five [points].
Second, the section clarifying the gate of that which is produced from the conditions of its accomplishment.
This also has three parts;
first, the question.
Next, the response indicates the characteristics;
subsequently, it provides the proof through scripture.
"What is the characteristic of the earth element within the internal dependent origination?"—this is the first question.
The Sūtra states:

"That which acts as solidity within this body is called the earth element," up to, "that which brings about the accomplishment of this sprout of name-and-form is called the consciousness element. These two demonstrate the characteristics; furthermore, they are divided into six.
First, the earth element;
second, the water element;
third, the fire element.
Fourth, the wind element;
fifth, the space element;
sixth, the consciousness element.
Sūtra:
That which acts as solidity within this body is called the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). This first clarifies the earth element.
Sūtra.
That which causes this body to cohere is called the water element (*ābdhātu*). These two clarify the water element;
for if the water element were absent within this body, it would perish.
The Sūtra states:
"That which can digest what the body eats, drinks, chews, and consumes is called the fire element (*tejodhātu*). This explains the fire element.
As for the term "food" (*āhāra*):
"Solid food" refers to various types of meals;
"drinks" refers to various kinds of syrups and the like.
"Chewing" refers to solid food;
"munching" refers to—
This refers to various foods and drinks;
for if the fire element were absent, they could not be transformed. Sūtra.
That which functions as the inhalation and exhalation within this body is called the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). These four clarify the wind element;
the scriptural passage is evident. [Sūtra] states:
That which creates vacuity and penetration within this body is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*). These five clarify the space element.
For if there were no space element, [the body] would be a solid unity.
Thus says the Sūtra:

The five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) in conjunction with [their objects] and the contaminated mental consciousness (*sāsrava-manovijñāna*)—just as the reed [supports the sprout]—that which is able to bring about this sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is called the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). These six clarify the element of consciousness.
The term "fivefold body of consciousness" refers to the five consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness.
The term "associated" refers to...
This refers to those factors associated with the five consciousnesses.
As for the mention of "outflow-tainted mental consciousness," it is because there is a portion that is outflow-free.
As for the expression "a bundle of reeds," this illustrates that the phenomena arising through conditions do not stand independently.
Sūtra:

If these various conditions do not exist, the body will not arise. If the internal earth element is not fully present, and likewise, if the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are not fully present, then as long as all these are combined, the body arises. These are the three proofs of establishment.
The scriptural passage can be seen as [expounding] the gate of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) arising from conditions without an agent.
It consists of four sections:
first, clarifying that the six conditions lack an agent.
Second, the fruit has no agent;
third, although there is no agent, the fruit is nevertheless accomplished;
fourth, the proof of this.

Sūtra: That earth element does not form the thought, "I am able to perform the function of solidity within the body. The water element does not form the thought, "I am able to perform the function of cohesion for the body. The fire element does not form the thought, "I am able to perform the function of digesting what the body eats, drinks, chews, and consumes. The wind element does not form the thought, "I am able to perform the function of internal and external inhalation and exhalation. The space element does not form the thought, "I am able to perform the function of creating voidness and permeability within the body. The consciousness element also does not form the thought, "I am able to bring about this sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that is the body. This first passage clarifies that among the six conditions, there is no agent.
The meaning of the sūtra is self-evident. The sūtra states:
"The body, moreover, does not form the thought, 'I am produced from these various conditions. Thus, these two fruits have no agent."
Sūtra:
"Nevertheless, when these various conditions are present, the body is immediately produced. [This means that] although these three lack an agent, their fruit is nevertheless accomplished.
Sūtra.

That earth element is also neither self, nor a sentient being, nor a life-force, nor a living soul, nor a human youth, nor an agent, nor male, nor female, nor a eunuch, nor autonomous, nor "mine," nor anything else; these are the four proofs.
For what reason do the various elements, such as earth and so forth, not form the thought:
"We constitute the qualities of hardness and so on within the body"?
It is for the sake of abandoning this view.
To say that the earth element is also not the self is to address that which is called "self," which is the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self.
It is designated as "self" because the nature of the various elements (*dhātu*) and so forth is not the self, for one is free from the conceit of "I";
yet it is also that very self.
Because they undergo repeated births within the various realms of existence (*gati*),
they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*);
whereas the elements (*dhātu*) such as earth and so forth are devoid of such realms and births.
It is not a sentient being.
Because there is a self,
that which exhausts its form and life-span is called "life" (jīva).
Because all phenomena are momentary, they are not a living being (*jīva*).
Because they are able to arise within the various realms of existence (*gati*),
they are termed "birth" (*jāti*).
Because it is free from a born agent, it is not something that is born.
As for the term "Māṇava," it refers to the various realms such as the earth and so forth, which arise from an agent.
Because he is devoid of an agent, he is not the "Māṇava" (the Youth).
One who clings to the existence of a capacity to act is called an "agent.
Because he is born from karma, he is not an agent.
Regarding the statement that they are "neither male, nor female, nor neuter":
this is because the various characteristics of males and so forth are established as horizontal designations based on the earth element and other such factors.
The statement "not mine" is for the purpose of abandoning the erroneous conception of "I" and "mine.
The statement "nor anything else," and so forth, [is for the same purpose].
Because it is not something created by Maheśvara or other such [causes].
The remainder of the scriptural text is explained as above. Fourth, the clarification of the essence (*tattva*).
The text is divided into seventeen sections.
Beginning from the analysis of the essence and meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the clarification of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of affliction,
the first section— the explanation of the essence of ignorance— consists of three parts.
First the question,
next the answer,
and finally the conclusion.
Sūtra: What is ignorance? This is the first question. Sūtra.

Regarding these six elements, to give rise to the notion of unity, the notion of a composite, the notion of permanence, the notion of solidity, the notion of indestructibility, the notion of bliss, and notions such as "a being," "a living soul," "a nourisher," "a person," "a youth," "an agent," "self," and "mine," as well as other various forms of ignorance—this is the second answer.
Regarding the "six elements," they are the earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
To give rise to the notion of non-differentiation regarding the distinctions among these six elements is called the "single notion."
The attachment to the view that the body is composed of atoms is called the "notion of a unified whole.
The attachment to the belief that what is subject to momentary change exists eternally [is called the notion of permanence].
This is called the notion of permanence.
To grasp at what was originally non-existent as now existing gives rise to the notion of spontaneity;
this is called the notion of solidity.
Having arisen, one again lacks attachment to the past; this is called the perception of non-destruction.
If one gives rise to a sense of peace and happiness regarding the eight liberations and the three concentrations, it is called the perception of peace and happiness.
Regarding "the life-force of sentient beings" (*jīva-jantu*):
the meaning is as explained previously;
it is because there is a self (*ātman*).
Because it can produce rebirth in the various realms of existence and nourishes this body,
it is called the "grasping of nourishment."
There is a person of great power and activity who moves and shifts within; therefore,
he is called a "person" (puruṣa).
What is called a "person" (pudgala) is also termed a "being who undergoes repeated existences" (sattva),
for they are able to go to various realms of existence (gati).
Because they receive various bodies such as those of humans and devas,
they are called "those who go and come" (pudgala).
This refers to, and includes, the various other forms of ignorance.
This is for the sake of [identifying] the grasper, the seer, the knower, and so forth.
Sūtra: "This is ignorance; these are the three fetters. Second, the clarification regarding formations (*saṃskāra*).
The text has two parts:
first, the explanation;
second, the conclusion.
The Sūtra states:
"Because there is ignorance, one gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion toward various objects. This is the first explanation;
it is because from greed, hatred, and delusion, the three types of action arise.
Sūtra:
"This is ignorance conditioned by formative forces"—these are the two fetters. Third, the explanation of consciousness has two parts.
1. Explanation.
2. Conclusion.
Sūtra.
That which is able to discern all objects is the first interpretation.
As for "all objects," this refers to forms, sounds, and so forth.
The Sūtra names this "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); these two constitute the first section. The fourth [section] clarifies "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), which consists of two parts.
First the analysis,
then the conclusion. Sūtra.
"Arising together with consciousness are the four aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*). This is the initial analysis.
As for the "four aggregates of clinging," they are the aggregates of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*).
Sūtra: "This is name-and-form; these two are the fetters. Sūtra: "The five knowledges and the six sense bases."
The various faculties based upon name-and-form are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); if name-and-form were absent, the six sense bases would lack a cause.

Sixth, contact (*sparśa*) is explained in the Sūtra: "The coming together of the three is called contact. By "the coming together of the three," one means the faculty, the object, and consciousness. Seventh, feeling (*vedanā*) is explained.
Sūtra:
That which experiences contact is called feeling (*vedanā*), because feeling arises from contact. Eighth, the clarification of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Sūtra:
Craving for sensation and attachment to it is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā); the ninth [link] clarifies "clinging" (upādāna).
The Sūtra states:
"That which increases craving is called clinging. The tenth [link] clarifies "existence" (bhava).
The Sūtra states:

"That which arises from grasping (*upādāna*) and is capable of producing karma is called existence (*bhava*). This is because that which is capable of producing karma is the proximate cause. [Next,] eleven [factors] clarify birth (*jāti*).
Sūtra:
The aggregates produced from those causes are called "birth"; as for the phrase "those causes," it refers to the proximate cause. 12. Explaining Old Age and Death, Sūtra:

The maturation of the aggregates once they have arisen is called aging; the disintegration of the aggregates once they have aged is called death. Since maturation is aging and disintegration is death, [the third aggregate] is thus established. Thirteen: the explanation of sorrow (*śoka*).
Sūtra:

At the time of death, that which is internally possessed of craving-attachment (*pariḍāha*) and feverish distress is called "sorrow" (*śoka*). By "craving-attachment," one means [attachment to] wives, children, and so forth. Fourteen: Explaining Lamentation (*parideva*).
Sūtra:
That which arises from sorrow and takes the form of various utterances is called lamentation. Fifteenth, the exposition of suffering.
Sūtra:

That which is experienced as bodily suffering by the five consciousnesses is called "suffering. By "the five consciousnesses," one means the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth; this reveals bodily suffering. The sixteenth [topic] clarifies grief (*daurmanasya*).
The Sūtra states:

"That which is experienced as suffering by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) through mental attention (*manasikāra*) is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*). To say "mental consciousness" refers to the sixth consciousness; this reveals the suffering of the mind. Seventeenth, the explanation of vexation (*upāyāsa*).
The Sūtra states:

"Those things such as these, along with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), are called 'distress' (*paryavasthāna*). Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it refers to royal attendants, merchants seeking profit, and so forth.
They are called "secondary afflictions" because they distress both body and mind.
This refers to anger, resentment, and so forth. Fifth, the explanation of the names consists of seventeen sections,
beginning with ignorance and ending with its affliction.
The meaning of the scriptural passage is self-evident.
It is called "great" because it has no beginning;
it is called "darkness" because it obscures the true nature.
It is called "formative" (*abhisaṃskāra*) because it constructs future existence;
it is called "discernment" (*vijñapti*) because it discerns all objects;
and it is called "mutual dependence" (*anyonyaniśraya*) because consciousness and the four aggregates depend upon one another.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that consciousness relies upon four bases;
namely, consciousness following form, and consciousness following feeling, perception, and formations.
As for the phrase "gate of arising":
It is called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because it serves as the gateway for the arising of the six consciousnesses;
it is called "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*) because it experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of prior karma.
It is because one is attached through craving for future existence.
As for "grasping," it is for the purpose of grasping future existence.
Furthermore, there are four of them:
namely, craving, grasping, views, and the grasping of precepts and observances, as well as the grasping of the view of self.
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to future existence":
Because it arises from existence (*bhava*).
